title: Is there a number the base five shapes cannot write?
description: The row of base five shapes grows as far as we like, and ordinary counting numbers are all broken into it. Then the board asks what shape would stand for an empty collection, and finds there is none to draw.
teaching_notes: One idea: every counting number can be grouped into landmarks, and new landmark symbols can always be made, but the number of objects in an empty collection has nothing to draw. Watch for students who say every number can be written because the row never ends.

video_script.why: The child uses the biggest-landmark-first method to see which numbers the base five shapes can write, and which cannot.
video_script.substitution: Instead of one number, the question asks about every number.
video_script.anchor: the book's base five shapes: triangle 1, square 5, hexagon 25, circle 125 and further landmarks
video_script.payoff_line: Yes, zero cannot be written, because the system has no shape for it.

final_answer.value: Yes: 0 cannot be represented, because the system has no symbol for it
final_answer.spoken: yes, zero cannot be written, because the system has no shape for it

hold_back: Yes: 0 cannot be represented, because the system has no symbol for it
maths_rules: landmarks 1, 5, 25, 125, 625, 3125, ...; each is 5 times the one before and the row never ends
any counting number: take the biggest landmark that fits, count it, subtract, and move down; the remainder is always smaller than that landmark, so it ends in triangles
a number bigger than every symbol so far needs only a new landmark, 5 times the last
0 is the number of objects in an empty collection; every written number needs at least one shape; 0 has no shape
check: 1 is 1 triangle, 4 is 4 triangles, 5 is 1 square; nothing in the row stands for 0
video_script.design: One idea: counting numbers always fit the row, but zero has no shape. The row of shapes stays on the board; an empty box appears at the end.

narration: <bookmark mark='row'/>We write a number by grouping it into landmarks, the same way as the example in your book.
<bookmark mark='count'/>A number tells how many objects are in a collection. A collection can also be empty.

beats.on_screen: To find: is there a number that cannot be written? Why?
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to say whether some number cannot be written, and why.

narration: <bookmark mark='fit'/>Step one, take any counting number. Take the biggest landmark that fits, and subtract it.
<bookmark mark='down'/>What is left is smaller than that landmark, so we move down a shape. We stop at triangles, which are worth one each.

beats.on_screen: a very big number needs a new landmark: 5 x (last landmark); new shape added to the row

marks.new: a new shape worth five times the last one is added

narration: <bookmark mark='big'/>Step two, think of a number bigger than every landmark we have.
<bookmark mark='new'/>We only need a new shape, worth five times the last one. We can always make one, so big numbers are never a problem.

narration: <bookmark mark='empty'/>Step three, think of the number of objects in an empty collection. That number is zero.
<bookmark mark='none'/>Every number in this system is written with at least one shape. For zero there is nothing to draw.

narration: <bookmark mark='check'/>Step four, check with small numbers. One is one triangle, four is four triangles, and five is one square. Zero matches no shape at all.

beats.on_screen: Answer: Yes: 0 cannot be represented, because the system has no symbol for it

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Yes, zero cannot be written, because the system has no shape for it.
<bookmark mark='rest'/>Every other counting number can be written, however big it is.
